Short-run values are not given because the meta-analytic short-run means could not be checked against the article.

## A.5 Uses: border adjustment, price floors and crediting {.unnumbered}

**The economics of border adjustment separates environmental equivalence from cost equivalence.** @keen2022bca show that non-price policies impose only the efficiency cost of abatement on firms, not the payment on remaining emissions, so they "generally impose markedly lower private costs on firms than carbon pricing (at equivalent shadow prices)". Charging imports the shadow price is then not a competitiveness response, and exemptions for non-price effort are justified on cooperation or leakage grounds rather than competitiveness. @mehling2019 anticipate adjusting border charges for effective carbon prices, explicit and implicit, computed from energy taxes by carbon content, average abatement cost times mandated reductions, or "economic models to identify the carbon price needed to achieve mandated emission reductions in a sector", with third-party verification. @cosbey2019 review design choices. The EU's mechanism deducts only the carbon price effectively paid, net of rebates and compensation [@EU2023; @EU2025Omnibus, Art. 9], and so does not recognize feebates or standards; paper 1.3 proposes recognizing the price signal [@StrettonWP13].

**No academic source measures policy-level crediting by a carbon-price equivalent.** Results-based climate finance pays for verified reductions, mostly by project. The crediting argument of paper 1.1 [@StrettonWP11] and the metric here are, as far as this review found, the first to pair the two.

## A.6 What is new here {.unnumbered}

**The concept of a carbon price equivalent, the idea of weighting by responsiveness and the representation of standards by shadow prices all precede this paper** [@black2022framework; @ParryBlackRoaf2021; @FischerNewell2008; @black2023cpat]. What this paper adds is: a closed-form, linear-in-policy TECP whose weights belong to the economy and can be published, with a corrected derivation from the CES cost function; a decomposition of every instrument into a switching and a demand margin; an exact and second-order version with a rule for when the closed form suffices; a theory of non-price instruments with identification assumptions; and a calibration that cites each source only for what it estimates, with an uncertainty band. The main objections a referee will raise are also in the literature: calibration fragility [@serletis2010ej; @havranek2012], tax salience [@li2014; @andersson2019], the difference between emission and cost equivalence [@keen2022bca; @goulder2016], and the failure of additivity under leakage and binding caps [@GoulderJacobsenvanBenthem2012]. @sec-calibration and @sec-limits address each.

# Appendix B: Derivations and proofs {.appendix .unnumbered}

*All results below were checked symbolically with sympy and numerically against the full nonlinear CES; `2.Source/verify_derivations.py` runs the 30 checks.*

## B.1 Proposition 1 {.unnumbered}

From @eq-exact, $\ln q'_{fs} = \ln q_{fs} - \sigma_s\ln P_{fs} + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)\ln(C'_s/C_s)$. At the baseline, $\partial\ln P_{fs}/\partial\pi_{gs} = \delta_{fg}$ and, by Shephard's lemma, $\partial\ln C_s/\partial\pi_{gs} = s_{gs}$. So $d\ln q_{fs} = -\sigma_s\pi_{fs} + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)\bar\pi_s = -\sigma_s(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) - \eta_s\bar\pi_s$, which is @eq-firstorder. The cut is $R_P = -\sum_{f,s}E_{fs}\,d\ln q_{fs} = \sum_s\big[\sigma_s\sum_f E_{fs}(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) + \eta_s E_s\bar\pi_s\big]$. By @eq-taus, $\sigma_s(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) = \sigma_s(x_{fs} - \kappa_s)\,\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}$ and $\eta_s\bar\pi_s = \eta_s\kappa_s\,\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s = \tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_s\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s$, which proves (i). For (ii), a \$1 tax gives $\pi_{fs} = x_{fs}$ and $\bar\pi_s = \kappa_s$, so $\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s = 1$. Since $E_{fs} = X_s s_{fs}x_{fs}$, $\sum_f E_{fs}(x_{fs} - \kappa_s) = X_s\big(\sum_f s_{fs}x_{fs}^2 - \kappa_s^2\big) = X_sV_s$, and $E_s\kappa_s = X_s\kappa_s^2$. So $\Lambda = \sum_s X_s(\sigma_sV_s + \eta_s\kappa_s^2)$, positive whenever some sector has $\eta_s > 0$ and positive emissions, or $\sigma_s > 0$ and $V_s > 0$. (iii) follows by dividing by $\Lambda$; the weights sum to $\Lambda/\Lambda = 1$. (iv) A tax $\tau$ gives $\pi_{fs} = \tau x_{fs}$, so both prices equal $\tau$ and $R_P = \tau\Lambda$.

## B.2 Proposition 2 {.unnumbered}

(i) $\sum_f s_{fs}\sigma_s(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) = \sigma_s(\bar\pi_s - \bar\pi_s) = 0$. At a cost minimum the elasticity of the CES aggregate with respect to each input equals its cost share, so $d\ln Q_s = \sum_f s_{fs}\,d\ln q_{fs}$ and the switching term contributes nothing to $Q_s$. For a uniform tax, $\sum_f s_{fs}\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \sigma_s(\kappa_s - \kappa_s) = 0$. (ii) With equal prices $p$ per unit of service, $s_{fs} = w_{fs}$, $x_{fs} = e_f/p$ and $\kappa_s = \bar e_s/p$, so $\sum_f q_{fs}\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = (\sigma_s Q_s/p)\sum_f w_{fs}(e_f - \bar e_s) = 0$. (iii) Under the old form, $d\ln q_{fs} = -\sigma_s(1-w_{fs})(e_f - \bar e_s)/p$ per dollar, so with equal prices $\sum_f q_{fs}\,d\ln q_{fs} = -(\sigma_sQ_s/p)\sum_f w_{fs}(1 - w_{fs})(e_f - \bar e_s) = (\sigma_sQ_s/p)\sum_f w_{fs}^2(e_f - \bar e_s)$, using $\sum_f w_{fs}(e_f - \bar e_s) = 0$. With equal shares $w_{fs} = 1/n$ this is $(1/n)\sum_f w_{fs}(e_f - \bar e_s) = 0$; in general it is not. With unequal prices the same argument applies to $\sum_f s_{fs}\,d\ln q_{fs}$; in the example's power sector it is $+0.13$ percent per dollar of tax, against $-0.16$ percent from the demand margin.

*Where the factor came from.* The Hicksian own-price elasticity of a CES input, holding the service constant, is $-\sigma_s(1 - s_{fs})$, and the cross-price elasticity is $\sigma_s s_{gs}$. A uniform tax changes every price, so fuel $f$'s response is $-\sigma_s(1-s_{fs})\pi_{fs} + \sigma_s\sum_{g\ne f}s_{gs}\pi_{gs} = -\sigma_s(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s)$. Earlier versions applied the own-price term alone to the price change relative to the mean, $-\sigma_s(1 - w_{fs})(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s)$, which drops the cross-price terms after the mean has already been subtracted, and used energy shares in place of cost shares.

## B.3 The normalization in version 0.2's appendix {.unnumbered}

Version 0.2's Appendix A.7 set $\tilde\varepsilon^{\,A7}_{fs} = \sigma_s(1-w_{fs})(e_f - \bar e_s)/p_{fs}$ and $\tilde\varepsilon^{\,A7}_s = |\eta_s|\bar e_s/C_s$, and A.9 set $\Lambda = \sum E_{fs}[\tilde\varepsilon^{\,A7}_{fs}(e_f - \bar e_s) + \tilde\varepsilon^{\,A7}_s\bar e_s]$, with the main text's intensive and extensive prices in dollars per unit of energy, $\Delta p_{fs} - \sum_g w_{gs}\Delta p_{gs}$ and $\sum_g w_{gs}\Delta p_{gs}$. A uniform tax then returns itself, because numerator and denominator coincide. But measure sector $s$'s energy in units $k$ times smaller: quantities scale by $k$, prices and emission factors by $1/k$, emissions are unchanged, $\tilde\varepsilon^{\,A7}$ is unchanged, and both the sector's terms in $\Lambda$ and its price wedges scale by $1/k$. The sector's weight relative to the other sectors therefore changes with the unit, and so does the TECP of any policy that is not a uniform tax: \$30.9 for the example's mix with power in megawatt-hours, \$30.1 in gigajoules. Under Proposition 1, $x_{fs} = e_f/p_{fs}$, $\kappa_s$ and $s_{fs}$ are unit-free and $\Lambda$ is in tonnes per dollar per tonne, so the TECP does not depend on units; the script checks this.

## B.4 Proposition 3 {.unnumbered}

(i) The CES is homothetic, so from any taxed price vector the response to a further tax has the form of Proposition 1 with cost shares, carbon per dollar and spending evaluated at that point: $R'(\tau) = \sum_s X_s(\tau)[\sigma_sV_s(\tau) + \eta_s\kappa_s(\tau)^2] > 0$. $R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, so $R(\tau^*) = R_P$ has at most one solution and bisection finds it. As $\tau \to \infty$ every emitting fuel's quantity goes to zero when $\eta_s > 0$. If a zero-carbon fuel exists and $\sigma_s > 1$, the cost index stays bounded and $q_{fs} \propto P_{fs}^{-\sigma_s}C_s^{\sigma_s - \eta_s} \to 0$. Otherwise every emitting fuel's price and the cost index rise in proportion to $\tau$, so $q_{fs}$ falls like $\tau^{-\eta_s}$; $\sigma_s = 1$ is the Cobb–Douglas limit of the same argument. So $R$ ranges over $[0, E)$ for $\tau \ge 0$, and over negative cuts for taxes down to the level at which a price reaches zero. At a finite horizon, $R_T(\tau)$ is increasing in the example and the script checks the bisection, but monotonicity is not guaranteed in general because partially adjusted quantities are off the CES optimum.

(ii) Expand @eq-exact to second order. With $u_{fs} = \ln P_{fs} = \pi_{fs} - \pi_{fs}^2/2 + O(\pi^3)$, $\ln(C'_s/C_s) = \frac{1}{1-\sigma_s}\ln\sum_f s_{fs}e^{(1-\sigma_s)u_{fs}} = \bar u_s + \tfrac{1-\sigma_s}{2}\mathrm{Var}_s(u) + O(\pi^3) = \bar\pi_s - \tfrac12\bar\pi_s^2 - \tfrac{\sigma_s}{2}V^\pi_s + O(\pi^3)$. So $\ln(q'_{fs}/q_{fs}) = L_{fs} + \tfrac12[\sigma_s\pi_{fs}^2 - (\sigma_s - \eta_s)(\bar\pi_s^2 + \sigma_sV^\pi_s)] + O(\pi^3)$, and $q'/q = 1 + \ln(q'/q) + \tfrac12 L_{fs}^2 + O(\pi^3)$. Summing $-E_{fs}$ times the second-order terms gives @eq-second. For the TECP, write $R(\tau) = \Lambda\tau + \tfrac12\Gamma\tau^2 + O(\tau^3)$ and $R_P = R^{(1)}_P + R^{(2)}_P + O(\pi^3)$. Substituting $\tau = \tau^*_{(1)} + \delta$ with $\delta$ of second order, $\Lambda\delta + \tfrac12\Gamma(\tau^*_{(1)})^2 = R^{(2)}_P$ to second order, which is @eq-tecp2; the residual is of third order. (iii) is the condition $\delta = 0$.

## B.5 Proposition 4 {.unnumbered}

Let the sector choose $q$ to minimize $\sum_f p_{fs}q_{fs}$ subject to $F(q) \ge Q_s$ and $\sum_f(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}})q_{fs} \le 0$. With multipliers $\mu$ and $\lambda$, the first-order conditions are $p_{fs} + \lambda(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}}) = \mu\,\partial F/\partial q_{fs}$, identical to those of minimizing $\sum_f[p_{fs} + \lambda(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}})]q_{fs}$ subject to $F(q) \ge Q_s$. Service demand responds to the cost index at these prices. Decentralized, each unit of fuel $f$ sold creates $\bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}} - e_f$ credits, negative for fuels above the standard, worth $\lambda$ each; competitive trading equalizes every supplier's marginal compliance cost at $\lambda$ [@Montgomery1972], and with full pass-through the delivered price is $p_{fs} + \lambda(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}})$. This proves (i) and (ii). (iii) Both routes produce the same cut in the same model, and Definition 1 depends only on the cut. (iv) A clean-share requirement $\sum_f(\theta - c_f)q_{fs} \le 0$, with $c_f = 1$ for clean and $0$ for fossil units, has the same structure, with price changes $\lambda(\theta - c_f)$.

## B.6 Proposition 5 {.unnumbered}

Applying Proposition 4 firm by firm, firm $i$ under its own binding standard chooses as if it faced a feebate at its own shadow price $\mu_i$ around its own standard. To first order its cut is $\mu_i$ times its cut per dollar of such a feebate, $E_ir_i\mu_i$. Summing over firms and dividing by $\Lambda$ gives the first expression in @eq-nontradable. Write $\bar r = \Lambda^F/E$ and $\bar\mu_E = \sum_iE_i\mu_i/E$ with $E = \sum_iE_i$. Then $\sum_iE_ir_i\mu_i = E[\bar r\bar\mu_E + \mathrm{Cov}_E(r,\mu)]$, which gives the second expression. (ii) is the case $\mathrm{Cov}_E = 0$. (iii) A tradable standard with the same cut has, by Definition 1, the same exact TECP, and by @Montgomery1972 it achieves the cut at least cost.

## B.7 Corollaries {.unnumbered}

*Corollary 1.* With $\Delta p_{fs} = t(e_f - \bar e_s)$, $\pi_{fs} = t(x_{fs} - \bar e_s/p_{fs})$ and $\bar\pi_s = t(\kappa_s - \bar e_s\sum_gs_{gs}/p_{gs})$, so $\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s = t[(x_{fs} - \kappa_s) - \bar e_s(1/p_{fs} - \sum_gs_{gs}/p_{gs})]$, and dividing by $x_{fs} - \kappa_s$ gives the stated intensive price. It equals $t$ for all $f$ if and only if $1/p_{fs} = \sum_gs_{gs}/p_{gs}$ for all $f$ (given $\bar e_s > 0$), that is, all prices are equal. Then $s_{fs} = w_{fs}$, $\kappa_s = \bar e_s/p$ and $\bar\pi_s = 0$.

*Corollary 2.* Replacing $\sigma_s$ and $\eta_s$ by $a^I_s(T)\sigma_s$ and $a^X_s(T)\eta_s$ in Proposition 1 scales each sector's switching and demand terms, in the policy's cut and in $\Lambda$ alike. With common speeds, $R_{P,T} = a^I\Lambda^I\tau^*_I + a^X\Lambda^X\tau^*_X$ and $\Lambda_T = a^I\Lambda^I + a^X\Lambda^X$; dividing and writing $\omega = \Lambda^I/\Lambda$ gives @eq-horizon. The first-order response at horizon $T$ follows from @eq-adjust because the switching and demand terms of @eq-firstorder are the long-run changes in $\ln h_{fs}$ and $\ln Q_s$, of which fractions $a^I_s(T)$ and $a^X_s(T)$ have occurred.

# Appendix C: CES and isoelastic forms; partial adjustment {.appendix .unnumbered}

*This appendix corrects and replaces Part II of version 0.2.*

## C.1 The CES system {.unnumbered}

With the aggregator @eq-ces, the unit cost is $C_s = (\sum_f\alpha_{fs}p_{fs}^{1-\sigma_s})^{1/(1-\sigma_s)}$ and conditional demand $q_{fs} = Q_s\alpha_{fs}(p_{fs}/C_s)^{-\sigma_s}$. Cost shares are $s_{fs} = \alpha_{fs}(p_{fs}/C_s)^{1-\sigma_s}$, so calibrating $\alpha_{fs}$ to observed shares and normalizing $C_s = 1$ at the baseline gives @eq-exact, in which the $\alpha_{fs}$ no longer appear. With service demand $Q_s \propto C_s^{-\eta_s}$, fuel demand is $q_{fs} \propto p_{fs}^{-\sigma_s}C_s^{\sigma_s - \eta_s}$. Version 0.2 wrote the exponent as $\sigma_s + \eta_s$ with $\eta_s$ negative; the two are the same. Year-by-year simulation applies @eq-exact relative to the previous year's quantities and prices, so the cost shares update as the mix changes.

## C.2 The elasticity matrix {.unnumbered}

Differentiating gives $\varepsilon_{ff} = -\sigma_s + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)s_{fs}$ and $\varepsilon_{fg} = (\sigma_s - \eta_s)s_{gs}$ for $g \ne f$. Holding the service fixed ($\eta_s = 0$), these are the Hicksian elasticities $-\sigma_s(1 - s_{fs})$ and $\sigma_s s_{gs}$. Each row sums to $-\eta_s$: a proportional rise in all prices cuts every fuel by the demand elasticity. Cross-price elasticities are proportional to the other fuel's cost share, and $s_{fs}\varepsilon_{fg} - s_{gs}\varepsilon_{gf} = 0$ in the Hicksian case (symmetry). The matrix is the isoelastic form the TECP uses to first order; version 0.2's Appendix A.6 stated it correctly, but its semi-elasticities in A.7 did not use it.

## C.3 Local equivalence and where the forms diverge {.unnumbered}

The isoelastic form $d\ln q_f = \sum_g\varepsilon_{fg}\pi_g$ is the first-order expansion of the CES at the baseline. It holds cost shares fixed; the CES lets them move. Version 0.2 stated that the linear form is accurate for price changes under about 20 percent. @sec-exact gives a sharper answer for the TECP: the relevant comparison is the curvature of the policy's cut against the benchmark tax's, which the second-order term measures directly. For emission cuts themselves, as opposed to the TECP, the linear form is poor well before 20 percent when a cheap, dirty fuel faces a large tax, as coal does in the example's industry.

## C.4 Partial adjustment {.unnumbered}

Version 0.2 adjusted quantities toward equilibrium at one speed (its A.4), or energy shares and total energy at separate speeds (A.5), and stated that the switching speed was 0.5–1.0 a year and the demand speed 0.05–0.10 while describing the fast one as conservation. Both the labels and the split are revised here. The fast speed belongs to the demand margin, which needs no new capital, and the slow speed to fuel switching, which follows the turnover of vehicles, boilers, furnaces and plants. The adjustment is applied to the two CES components, $\ln h_{fs}$ and $\ln Q_s$ (@eq-adjust), rather than to energy shares and total energy, so the switching margin stays on the isoquant at every date and the horizon TECP of Corollary 2 follows directly. Adjusting in logs keeps quantities positive and makes the horizon elasticities $a(T)$ times the long-run ones, which is what the identity $\lambda \approx \varepsilon^{SR}/\varepsilon^{LR}$ assumes. The half-life of adjustment is $\ln 2/\ln(1/(1-\lambda))$, about 2 years for the demand margin at $\lambda^X = 0.35$ and 10 years for switching at $\lambda^I = 0.07$. Speeds may differ by sector and by fuel pair; switching between gasoline and diesel vehicles is faster than between gas boilers and heat pumps.

## C.5 Technical efficiency {.unnumbered}

Expressing quantities in useful energy multiplies each fuel's quantity by its conversion efficiency $\varphi_{fs}$ and divides its price and emission factor by $\varphi_{fs}$. Spending, emissions, cost shares and carbon per dollar are unchanged, so $\Lambda$, the weights and every TECP are unchanged. Efficiency matters for the interpretation of Proposition 2(ii), where "equal prices" means equal prices per unit of useful energy, and for the substitution elasticity, which should be estimated over useful energy where an efficient fuel replaces an inefficient one, as electricity replaces gasoline in vehicles.

# Appendix D: Code, data and calibration {.appendix .unnumbered}

**Code.** All scripts are in `2.Source/` and run with Python 3, NumPy, SymPy and Matplotlib.

- `tecp_model.py`: the nested CES, instruments as price changes, first-order, second-order and exact TECPs, the credit price of the fuel standard and partial adjustment. Its `check_against_brief()` asserts that it reproduces the brief's numbers (credit price \$166, first-order TECP \$33.21, exact \$36.86, $\Lambda$ = 1.5947 Mt per dollar per tonne).
- `verify_derivations.py`: 30 symbolic and numerical checks of Propositions 1–5, Corollaries 1–2, the second-order expansion, the old $(1 - w)$ form and version 0.2's appendix normalization, and finite-difference checks against the full nonlinear CES.
- `make_wp_figures.py`: @fig-weights to @fig-horizon and `figures/wp_numbers.md`, which lists every number quoted in the text. The Monte Carlo uses 2,000 draws with seed 20261029.

The brief's script, `1.Presentation/figures/make_figures.py`, uses the same economy.

**Data.** @tbl-economy gives the stylized economy. Delivered prices include existing taxes; power prices are levelized costs per MWh.

Sector totals: power 119.0 Mt, spending \$14.6 billion, $\kappa$ = 8.2 kg per dollar, $\sigma$ = 2.0, $\eta$ = 0.2; road transport 80.4 Mt, \$34.7 billion, 2.3 kg, $\sigma$ = 1.5, $\eta$ = 0.4; industry 62.0 Mt, \$7.9 billion, 7.8 kg, $\sigma$ = 0.8, $\eta$ = 0.3. All values stylized. {#tbl-economy}

**Instruments.** The carbon tax adds \$30 times the emission factor to each fuel's price in power and industry. The subsidy lowers the price of renewable power by \$10 per MWh. The fuel standard requires road fuels' carbon intensity per unit of energy to be 2 percent below its baseline (0.0668 t/GJ); its credit price is the $\lambda$ at which the constraint binds in the full model, and its price changes are $\lambda(e_f - 0.0668)$.

**Monte Carlo.** Each draw takes $\sigma_s$ and $\eta_s$ independently and uniformly from the ranges in @tbl-calibration, re-solves the standard's credit price, and computes first-order and exact TECPs for each instrument and the mix. One-year draws also take $\lambda^I$ and $\lambda^X$ uniformly from their ranges and hold the standard at its long-run credit price for that draw: a 2 percent intensity cut cannot be met within one year in this model at any credit price that keeps the biofuel price positive, so a standard required to bind at once would trade at its price ceiling.

**The workbook.** `2.Source/PolicyEquivalentCarbonPriceAndCES.xlsx` implements version 0.2, with the $(1 - w)$ semi-elasticities and a two-sector example. It is superseded by the scripts above and kept for its dynamic simulation layout.
